name: Coffee shop business
blurb: Open a café or coffee bar selling espresso drinks, filter coffee and simple food
title: Coffee Shop Business: How to Open a Coffee Shop
description: How to open a coffee shop: how a café makes money, the lease, equipment and permits it needs, who it suits, the rent and franchise traps, and how to test first.
h1: How to open a coffee shop
answer: A coffee shop sells espresso drinks, filter coffee and usually some food from a café, kiosk or cart. The coffee in each cup is cheap; rent, staff, equipment and the fit-out are not, and many first cafés struggle because the lease and wages outrun the number of cups they sell.

sections.h: How a coffee shop makes money
body: Customers pay per drink, with food, beans, merchandise and catering adding to each visit. Morning rush hours often bring most of the day's trade.

Costs include rent, wages, coffee, milk, food, cups, utilities, equipment servicing, card fees and, for franchises, royalties. Customers who sit for hours with one drink also take seats from paying customers.

ul: A site with foot traffic at the times people buy coffee, and a lease you have read in full.
Equipment: espresso machine, grinders, water filtration, fridges, dishwasher and a point-of-sale system. Used gear can cut costs if it is serviced.
Permits and food safety: rules differ by country and city. Examples include a business licence, food premises registration, health inspection, signage permits and fire checks.
Bean and milk suppliers, and food you can make or buy in safely.
Barista skills, staff, and insurance for property and public liability.

sections.h: Who it suits (and who it doesn't)

head: Suits
Not for
rows: People who have worked in cafés and know the pace
Anyone who has never worked a busy coffee bar
Owners ready to work early mornings for the first year
People wanting a semi-retired lifestyle business
Sites near offices, transit, schools or busy streets
Anyone without savings for a slow start

ul: Rent and long leases: the most common way a first café gets into trouble.
Staffing: wages, scheduling and turnover take more time than most owners expect.
Franchise pitches: in the US, the FTC says franchisors must hand over a disclosure document at least 14 days before you sign or pay; read the fees and talk to current owners.
Buying an existing café: check real sales records, equipment condition and the lease that comes with it.
Competition from chains and from cafés that open nearby after you.

sections.h: How to test it cheaply first

ol: Work some shifts in a busy café if you have not before.
Count passers-by and nearby coffee shops at your target street in the morning.
Run a coffee cart or market stall, where permits allow, to test prices and drinks.
Get quotes for rent, fit-out and equipment for one candidate site.
Work out how many cups a day pay for rent and wages; stop if the number looks out of reach.
Have a lawyer read the lease before signing, and negotiate fit-out time.
Get permits, inspections and insurance in place.
Open with a short menu you can serve fast and consistently.
Get listed on maps with correct hours and photos.
Track daily sales by hour, waste and wages, and adjust staffing to busy times.

faq.q: Is a coffee cart a good way to start?
faq.a: It can be. A cart or kiosk costs less than a full café and tests your drinks and pricing, but you still need food permits and a spot with enough morning foot traffic.

faq.q: Should I buy a coffee shop franchise?
faq.a: A franchise brings a brand and systems but adds fees, royalties and rules. Read the full disclosure document, ask an accountant to review it and speak to current and former franchisees.
Most often, costs that are too high for the trade the site brings in: rent, wages and a fit-out funded by debt. Check those numbers before you sign anything.
